text: This is the story of Rome falling from Republic to Empire. We always focus on the individuals, the Marius, the Sulla, the Pompeys, the Caesars. But actually the reason it fell was the system. The Roman system became more and more outdated. It never adapted to what happened when they conquered the world. When they conquered the world they created more and more wealth for the top end of society and they created a massive influx of slave labour. The small farmer, who was the backbone of the Roman army, is pushed off the land and poor. We get all these populist politicians who are promising land, grain, glory to the people. And then the loyalty of the army shifts from the state to the commander. And so we get these huge civil wars. And the system was broken. It's not that Sulla suddenly becomes a dictator or Caesar suddenly crosses the Rubicon. It is an already very unstable system that is very prone to violence, vetoes, breaking of norms. And the economy and the system and the military structure all reinforced one another. Of course individual personalities mattered. Caesar's ambition, Pompey's vanity, the senate's unwillingness to compromise turned it into civil wars. And Rome could have survived, that's not destined. If they had the will to reform and reform land and citizenship and military command before they were so used to winning or losing by war. But in the end, Octavian becomes the principate and it turns into an autocracy. And the lesson to be learned is that a system which does not reform itself, a political system will eventually collapse into those who bring stability through force.
